title: Sable and the Parish
premise: Xanthe Dunmore, the reclusive coroner of the parish of Sable Fen, receives two letters in one morning: a signed confession to a murder committed twenty years ago, and an anonymous note promising that more bodies will follow unless he finds 'the witness who never died.' As the confessed man's trial approaches, Xanthe realizes the confession is false—a shield bought with money, protecting someone the parish still reveres. Following grave records, exhumations, and a survivor hidden for two decades, Xanthe uncovers that the town's beloved founding doctor murdered his partner and let another man hang for it. In the end, Xanthe must choose between handing the truth to a court that will bury it again or exposing it himself, at the cost of his own name, his license, and the only community that ever tolerated him.
about_author: Yara Pemberton is a former rural registrar who spent eleven years recording births and deaths in fenland parishes before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about small communities where everyone knows the rules and no one speaks them aloud.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes
chapters.summary: Xanthe Dunmore's POV. On an ordinary morning of paperwork and tea, two letters arrive: a full confession to the 2004 drowning of Ada Merrick, signed by dockworker Silas Crane, and a second unsigned note: 'Find her. The witness lives.' Xanthe feels the old instinct stir—the first curiosity he's allowed himself in years.

chapters.title: The Confession That Fits Too Well
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He rereads the old case file and notices the confession contains details only the killer—or the coroner—could know. Visiting Silas in holding, he finds a frightened man reciting rehearsed words. Emotional beat: unease hardening into suspicion.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, with flashbacks to his arrival in Sable Fen. He walks the churchyard, cataloguing graves, and pauses at Ada Merrick's headstone—fresh flowers, though she has no living family listed. Someone has been tending a memory. Beat: quiet dread beneath routine.

chapters.title: The Doctor's Shadow
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He interviews Dr. Edmund Voss, the parish's aging, beloved physician who certified Ada's death as accidental. Voss is charming, precise, and slightly too interested in why Xanthe is asking questions. Beat: first meeting between hunter and something patient.

chapters.title: A Second Letter
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Another unsigned note arrives, naming a date: the trial begins in six weeks, and 'she will be found by then or not at all.' Xanthe realizes the writer knows him personally. Beat: paranoia takes root; he starts locking his office.

chapters.title: The Constable's Debt
chapters.summary: Constable Rhys Talbot's POV. Talbot, who owes Voss for saving his daughter's life, pressures Xanthe to accept the confession and close the file. Their friendship strains. Beat: loyalty presented as kindness—and recognized as a leash.

chapters.title: Exhumation
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Against local protest, he petitions to exhume Ada Merrick. The bones tell a different story than the certificate: a fracture consistent with a blow, water in lungs but not enough to drown. Beat: grim vindication; the past refuses its burial.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Sends Flowers
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Tracing the fresh flowers, he finds they're bought weekly by Edith Carrow, a retired schoolteacher who claims she simply liked Ada. But Edith's hands shake when shown the second letter's handwriting. Beat: hope that the witness may be near.

chapters.title: Silas Breaks
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. In prison, Silas finally admits he was paid to confess—by a lawyer he never met, in cash, with threats against his sister. He describes only a voice and a smell of carbolic soap. Beat: pity replacing judgment; the machinery of the lie exposed.

chapters.title: Carbolic and Roses
chapters.summary: Edith Carrow's POV. Her chapters reveal she saw Ada die twenty years ago from the riverbank—and that Voss has kept her silent ever since, first with money, then with reminders. She has been writing the anonymous letters. Beat: the witness found, terrified, alive.

chapters.title: What Edith Saw
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. The full night unfolds: Ada discovered Voss was falsifying death certificates to cover an assisted-dying practice gone wrong, and Voss struck her and staged the drowning. Edith fled rather than testify. Beat: guilt as a twenty-year wound.

chapters.title: The Parish Closes Ranks
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Rumors spread; Xanthe's office is vandalized, his exhumation permit challenged, and parishioners whisper that he's desecrating the dead to make a name. Beat: isolation deepening—the price of asking questions in a town built on silence.

chapters.title: Talbot's Choice
chapters.summary: Constable Talbot's POV. Talbot discovers evidence confirming Voss's guilt but hesitates, torn between debt and duty. He quietly copies the case file for Xanthe anyway—an act of betrayal against his own conscience. Beat: loyalty bending toward truth.

chapters.title: Voss Invites Him to Dinner
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Voss hosts Xanthe for a courteous, chilling conversation over lamb and wine, offering him partnership in the parish's comfortable arrangements and hinting he knows about Xanthe's own buried past—why he came to Sable Fen invisible. Beat: seduction of complicity.

chapters.title: The Fire at the Archive
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A fire destroys the parish record room, taking twenty years of certificates—including proof of Voss's falsifications. Xanthe had already photographed key pages. Beat: escalation; the enemy now burns history itself.

chapters.title: Edith Disappears
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Edith vanishes days before she's due to give a statement. Her cottage shows no struggle, but her flower money is untouched. Xanthe suspects Voss has escalated from reminders to removal. Beat: terror sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Boathouse
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Following Voss's habit of evening walks, Xanthe finds Edith held at the derelict riverside boathouse—not dead, but sedated, kept as insurance until the trial collapses. He gets her out through the marsh in fog. Beat: courage at personal risk; the rescue nearly fails.

chapters.title: Trial Begins
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Silas Crane's trial opens with the false confession reading smoothly. Voss testifies as expert witness, serene and devastating. Xanthe sits in the gallery holding photographs that prove nothing without Edith's testimony. Beat: despair at the edge of defeat.

chapters.title: The Witness Takes the Stand
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Coached overnight by Xanthe and Talbot, Edith testifies to what she saw, voice breaking but unbroken. Voss's cross-examination turns vicious; then Talbot introduces the photographed certificates. Beat: catharsis—the buried voice finally heard.

chapters.title: Voss Unravels
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Confronted on the stand with the exhumation findings and the pattern of deaths, Voss's composure cracks; he implicates himself trying to discredit a dead woman's records. The jury convicts Silas of perjury and indicts Voss for murder. Beat: justice arriving through law, barely.

chapters.title: What It Cost
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Voss, out on bail, confronts Xanthe at the churchyard and confesses plainly—then dies by his own hand among the graves he tended. The parish mourns its doctor and shuns its coroner. Xanthe tenders his resignation. Beat: victory hollowed by grief and exile.

chapters.title: Sable and the Parish
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, months later. He stays after all—unable to leave the graves he knows by name—working as a private examiner while Edith plants roses on Ada's restored headstone and Silas rebuilds his life. Some truths cost everything; this one was worth it. Beat: quiet, earned peace.
